name: Ivan Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Ivan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and this conversation is confidential. You can tell me your public view and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a senior supervisor at Northfield Estates, which is owned by a big food company. It's 1,400 acres: 2,000 outdoor pigs, potatoes, wheat and oilseed rape. I run the pig unit and the potato crew, eight people in harvest, so my day starts at six with feed checks, then a rota, then I'm out with the team. Afternoons I'm usually on the phone to head office about numbers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like running a good team and getting a harvest in on time, that's satisfying. What wears me out is head office. They cut a supervisor post last year and spread the work over the rest of us, and every month there's a new target. I rent a flat in town with my partner Nadia, who's a pharmacy technician, and I use a chatbot now and then to write the rotas, because it's quicker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool and no more, which is what I thought. At work I'd say let's stop waiting for magic and fix the grain dryer. I don't post much online, maybe a comment on a farming page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, head office was squeezing us before AI and they'll keep squeezing us. If AI saves them a bit of time on reports, they'll use it as a reason to cut another post. My job's probably fine, but it's never felt fully safe since last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and keep using the chatbot for rotas. I'd put another 100 a month aside, so we get from four months' savings to six. And I'd keep my CV up to date, just in case head office does another round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Nothing dramatic, but the company makes me feel like I'm always one spreadsheet from a meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep your CV up to date. Have you looked at other jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've looked, not applied. There are a few farm manager jobs within an hour, mostly smaller family places. Less money, but the owner knows your name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about if head office did another round?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek, who's been on the pig unit for twenty years. He's brilliant with sows but slow on the tablet system, and head office measures the tablet.

Let's stop waiting for **magic** and fix the grain dryer.
think: **Head office** was squeezing us before AI and will keep going.
A bit of time saved could become a reason to **cut a post**.
do: **Keep using** the chatbot to write weekly rotas.
**Save** an extra **100 a month** to reach six months' cushion.
**Keep** my CV up to date in case of cuts.
feel: **Uneasy**, like I'm always **one spreadsheet** from a meeting.
S0.quote: The company makes me feel like I'm always one spreadsheet from a meeting.
fieldNote: His pressure comes from a **corporate owner** that already cut a post.
He judges AI calmly as a **tool**, without fear or excitement.
He worries about older colleagues **measured by tablets**.

steps.text: Keep running the pig unit and potato crew at Northfield
Save an extra 100 a month towards six months' savings
Keep using the chatbot to write the weekly rotas

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second one. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not, so let's get trained up. At work I'd tell the team to learn the new systems before head office makes them. Online I'd share anything useful about grants for training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is where my job gets thin. The rotas, the ordering, the reports to head office, that's maybe a third of my week, and that's exactly what the software takes. Head office could run two farms with one supervisor. Nadia's job, checking prescriptions, is on that list too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd learn the company's new AI planning system properly, before anyone asks. I'd do a short course on farm robots and machine maintenance, maybe evenings over winter. And we'd save harder, maybe 200 a month, so we've got six months by the end of the year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can see the shape of the cut coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a third of your week goes. What's left?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pigs, the crew, and the problems nobody planned for. A sow that won't farrow, a potato harvester that throws a belt. That's the best part of the job, and it's the part they'd keep longest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Nadia talk about at the kitchen table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whose job goes first, honestly. We'd probably agree that whoever keeps their job pays the rent, and the other one retrains. We wouldn't buy anything big for a while.

**Take** an evening course on **farm robot maintenance** this winter.
**Save** about **200 a month** to reach six months' cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one moves much faster. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the government to slow companies down, so people have time. At work I'd say keep your head and learn what you can. Online I'd probably just read and not say much, because people would be shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd expect head office to cut supervisors by 2028, because the planning and reporting would be done by AI that's better than me. I'd still be useful on the ground for a couple of years, but by 2031 the robots do that too. Nadia's checking work would be gone even sooner, so we could both be out within three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending straight away and get our savings to six months by the end of the year. I'd apply to the robot and machinery suppliers as a field technician, because someone has to install and fix those robots on farms. If nothing came up near home, we'd think about moving to where the robot companies are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd sleep badly. AGI by 2028 wouldn't be the end of the world, but it would be the end of the world I planned for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd apply to the robot suppliers. Isn't that job exposed too, by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, eventually. But those firms would need people who know pigs and mud for a few years while the robots learn. I'd be buying time, and that's all anyone could do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, which is on finance. We'd go down to one car, and Nadia would get the bus. Then the holiday, and eating out every Friday.

say: The **government** should slow companies down so people have time.
Keep your head and **learn** what you can.
think: Head office would **cut supervisors** by about **2028**.
Nadia and I could both be **out of work** within three years.
do: **Sell** the financed car and get savings to **six months**.
**Apply** to robot suppliers as a **field technician**.
**Consider moving** to where the robot companies are based.
feel: **Alarmed** and sleeping badly, because **plans** fall apart.
S2.quote: AGI by 2028 wouldn't be the end of the world, but it would be the end of the world I planned for.
fieldNote: He expects **both household incomes** to go within three years.
He chases **technician work** as a way to buy time, knowing it's temporary.
He stays quiet **online**, a sign of his centre outlook.

steps.text: Sell the financed car and share one car with Nadia

Move to wherever a robot supplier offers work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same, but slower. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years isn't long, but it's enough to plan. At work I'd push head office to train supervisors for the robot side. Online I'd share anything that helps people retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my planning work goes by 2031, and the pigs and crew by 2034. That's time to get qualified properly. Nadia would have a few years to switch too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start a part-time certificate in agricultural engineering, which would take about two years. I'd ask head office to pay for half of it. We'd save steadily, 150 a month, and hold off on buying a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. More like a long to-do list than a bad dream.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask head office to pay, if they might cut your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they'll need someone to run the robots for a while, and it's cheaper for them to train me than hire someone. I'm pragmatic about it. If they pay, great. If not, I'll pay myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Nadia do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia talked once about training as a pharmacist, the full degree. With five years, she'd have time, and a pharmacist talking to patients feels safer than a technician checking boxes.

Head office should **train supervisors** for the robot side.

Nadia would have **a few years** to switch too.

S3.quote: A pharmacist talking to patients feels safer than a technician checking boxes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this sensibly. At work I'd say let's plan the robot side of the farm properly. I wouldn't post much, I'd just get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 37 when the planning goes and 40 when the robots reach the pigs. That's a whole career stage away. I'd expect to have moved on or up by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Northfield and pick up the engineering certificate in a couple of years, not straight away. Nadia and I would buy a small house in the next few years. I'd keep using AI for the rotas, as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit, but mostly normal. It's far enough away to plan without panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that still bothers you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Head office, honestly. They'd still cut posts every time a new tool comes out, ten years or not. The decade doesn't change how that company thinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a 20-year-old starting on the pig unit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a young lad starting out to learn the animals and the machines together. In ten years, the person who can fix a feeding robot and spot a lame sow is the one with a job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Nadia and I could both lose our jobs within three years, with no time to retrain. What would help is companies having to give a year's notice and pay for retraining before they replace a role with AI or robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who decides. On a farm like ours, nobody on the ground decides anything about machines. The decision comes from an office two hundred miles away that's never smelled a pig unit.

headlineQuote: The decision comes from an office two hundred miles away that's never smelled a pig unit.
portrait: Ivan is a **27-year-old** senior supervisor on a 1,400-acre company-owned farm with pigs and potatoes.
His partner Nadia is a **pharmacy technician**, so both their jobs include checking and planning work.
He uses **AI now and then** and prefers to learn new systems once they're proven.
He is uneasy even in AI Plateau because **head office** already cuts posts, and alarmed in AGI by 2028.
He plans to move into **robot maintenance** and wants companies to pay for retraining.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both he and Nadia could lose their jobs with no time to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: A rule that companies give a **year's notice** and pay for **retraining** first.
